questions.question: US imports Russian diesel by October 31?

On October 9, 2026, Donald Trump announced an agreement with Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel fuel, and the United States Treasury issued General License 135 authorizing the importation of Russian-origin diesel fuel into the United States through April 7, 2027 (see: https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117412435306815143 & https://ofac.treasury.gov/recent-actions/20261009_33).

Russian diesel fuel refers to diesel fuel of Russian production origin.

Imported to the United States refers to the diesel fuel being physically delivered to a United States port or into the terrestrial territory of the United States for commercial or government use within the United States. Diesel fuel carried as a vessel’s own fuel, held in bond for re-export, or passing through the United States in transit to another country will not qualify.

To qualify, the import must either be described by a consensus of credible reporting as having been made under the agreement announced on October 9, 2026 (or any amended or successor arrangement between the governments of the United States and Russia), or be authorized under General License 135 (or any amended or successor authorization permitting the importation of Russian-origin diesel fuel).

The primary resolution source for this market will be a consensus of credible reporting.

This market will resolve according to the margin of victory between the top two candidates in the second round of the next Brazil Presidential Election.

For the purpose of this market, the “margin of victory” is defined as the absolute difference between the percentages of valid votes received by the first- and second-place candidates. Percentages of the valid votes received by each candidate will be determined by dividing the total number of valid votes each of the top two candidates receives by the sum of all valid votes cast in the election.

If the reported value falls exactly between two brackets, then this market will resolve to the higher range bracket.

If a candidate other than Flávio Bolsonaro or Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva receives the most valid votes in the second round, or if the top two candidates receive exactly the same number of valid votes, this market will resolve to "Other".

This market will resolve based on the official vote count once the vote count has been made official.

If a recount is initiated before the vote total has been made official, the market will remain open until the recount is completed and the vote is made official.

If the result of this election isn't known definitively by June 30, 2027, 11:59 PM ET, the market will resolve to "Other".

This market will resolve based on the result of the election, as indicated by a consensus of credible reporting. If there is ambiguity, this market will resolve based solely on the official results as reported by the Brazilian government, specifically the Superior Electoral Court (Tribunal Superior Eleitoral, TSE) (e.g., https://dadosabertos.tse.jus.br/).

forecasts.rationale: Trump said on Sept 22 he was looking very seriously at a diesel export ban with diesel at a record $6.52, and Treasury said it was examining one. The White House then denied on Sept 23 that it was preparing a ban, and Energy Secretary Wright said nobody was considering a flat ban because it could raise gasoline and jet prices; the oil industry opposes it. On Oct 9 the administration took the opposite tack, licensing Russian diesel imports through April 2027. A federal export ban announced by Nov 3 is possible only if prices spike again.

Base rate for a US diesel export ban is near zero historically. The White House explicitly denied considering a ban on Sept 23, with Energy Secretary Wright citing adverse price effects on gasoline and jet fuel, and the administration instead licensed Russian diesel imports on Oct 9 as its chosen price-relief measure. With only ~3 weeks until the midterms, reversing course to announce and implement a ban would be politically and policy-inconsistent. Only a sudden, severe supply crisis could change this, but current evidence points decisively to NO.

The base rate for a federal diesel export ban in the U.S. is very low, as such measures are rare and typically only considered during severe supply crises. Although Trump and some officials expressed serious consideration in late September, the White House explicitly denied pursuing a ban on September 23 and instead opted to license Russian diesel imports through April 2027 to ease prices, indicating a policy direction opposite to a ban. With the midterms only a few weeks away and no credible signs of an imminent ban, the probability remains low, though a sudden price spike or political shift could modestly raise it.

US diesel export bans are historically rare, and the White House explicitly denied considering one in late September, while the Energy Secretary warned it could raise gasoline and jet fuel prices. The administration has instead licensed Russian diesel imports to ease prices before the midterms, indicating a chosen alternative. Only a sharp reversal and emergency action before Nov 3 would make this Yes, so I assign a low but non-zero probability.

Base rate for U.S. diesel export bans is near zero, as they are historically rare and opposed by the petroleum industry. The White House explicitly denied considering a ban after Trump floated it, Energy Secretary Wright warned it could raise gasoline and jet fuel prices, and the administration instead licensed Russian diesel imports on Oct. 9 as its chosen pre-midterm price relief. With only about three weeks until the election, the window for a dramatic policy reversal is narrow, though an unexpected surge in diesel prices could theoretically revive the proposal.

The base rate for a sudden federal diesel export ban is very low, and the White House explicitly denied considering one on Sept 23. The Oct 9 decision to license Russian diesel imports is a concrete alternative that reduces the political need for an export embargo. A late Trump reversal remains possible if prices stay high before the midterms, but current evidence points to no ban.

The base rate for a sudden major policy reversal in the final ~21 days before an election is low. The White House explicitly denied considering a diesel export ban on Sept 23, Energy Secretary Wright warned it would spike gasoline and jet fuel prices, and the API opposed it. Critically, on Oct 9 the administration chose an alternative solution—licensing Russian diesel imports through April 2027—signaling its preferred approach to easing prices. However, diesel remains at $6.28/gal, keeping political pressure elevated, so a last-minute reversal cannot be entirely ruled out.

questions.question: Diesel export ban before midterms?
questions.resolution_criteria:
Resolution criteria

This market will resolve to YES if the United States federal government enacts a ban or embargo on the export of diesel fuel (distillate fuel oil) from the U.S. at any point before the U.S. midterm elections on November 3, 2026. Otherwise, this market will resolve to NO.

To qualify:

The action must be federal, implemented via an executive order, a federal agency action (e.g., from the Department of Energy or the Bureau of Industry and Security), or federal legislation signed into law. State-level proposals, actions, or non-binding resolutions do not qualify.

The policy must legally prohibit or comprehensively restrict the export of U.S. diesel fuel to foreign markets (temporary bans or short-term emergency embargoes qualify, but narrow, non-binding guidelines or routine administrative export licensing adjustments do not).

The ban must be officially announced and scheduled to take effect or be in effect prior to November 3, 2026.

Credible financial and political news sources—such as Bloomberg, Reuters, or The Wall Street Journal—will be used to verify the outcomes.

forecasts.rationale: El-Sayed is the Democratic nominee in a toss-up Michigan Senate race against Mike Rogers, leading by 1-7 points in six recent polls (InsiderAdvantage Oct 9-10: 48-46). He has repeatedly appeared with Hasan Piker, including a final primary event on Aug 3, and when asked on Oct 12 dismissed the line of questioning as silly rather than distancing himself. An explicit condemnation or disavowal would cost him the base in a close race, so it is unlikely before Nov 3 unless a new Piker controversy forces it.

Base rate for candidates in tight races disavowing controversial figures in final weeks is moderate (~30%), but El-Sayed has consistently dismissed Piker questions since August without disavowing, suggesting a strategic choice to avoid alienating progressive voters. The Toss-Up race and pressure from Jewish leaders/Democrats create incentive, but with only 3 weeks left and a slight polling lead, a reversal would risk appearing calculating and depressing youth turnout. A major new Piker controversy or polling shift could trigger a statement, but current trajectory favors maintaining the 'dismiss as silly' stance.

The base rate for candidates issuing explicit disavowals of controversial supporters before an election is roughly 30%. El‑Sayed has so far dismissed concerns about Hasan Piker without disavowing him, showing reluctance, but ongoing criticism from Jewish leaders and Michigan Democrats could create pressure. His current lead in the polls reduces the incentive to take a risky move, lowering the likelihood somewhat.

The base rate for a candidate explicitly disavowing a controversial former associate mid-campaign is low, as it risks alienating supporters. El-Sayed has consistently dismissed calls to condemn Piker, most recently on Oct 12, and with the election only three weeks away, he likely calculates that a disavowal would do more harm than good in a tight race. However, if external pressure from Jewish leaders or Democratic officials intensifies, he might still issue a statement, so the probability is not negligible.

Candidates rarely explicitly condemn a progressive ally who helped them win a primary unless a major new scandal forces their hand. El-Sayed dismissed Piker-related questions as 'silly' on October 12 and has resisted months of pressure from Michigan Democrats and Jewish leaders, suggesting he sees disavowal as costlier than the ongoing controversy. With only three weeks until polls close and El-Sayed holding a narrow lead, a last-minute reversal would risk alienating his base and appearing opportunistic without clear electoral benefit. The probability would rise only if Piker generates a severe new controversy or polling shows the association is decisively sinking El-Sayed with swing voters.

The base rate for a candidate formally disavowing a past campaign ally is low unless the ally becomes a major liability or new scandal emerges. The evidence lowers the probability because El-Sayed is polling ahead and, as of Oct. 12, was still refusing to disavow Piker and dismissing comparisons. The probability could rise if Piker says or does something new, if Jewish-voter pressure intensifies, or if the campaign decides an apology for the joint events is strategically necessary.

El-Sayed has had months since the primary events to distance himself from Piker but has consistently refused, dismissing criticism as 'silly' as recently as Oct 12. Politicians leading in polls rarely disavow allies who helped them in primaries, as it risks alienating the progressive base while not gaining moderate votes. With only ~3 weeks remaining and El-Sayed already up 1-7 points, the incentive to create a controversy by formally condemning Piker is very low; a YES would require either a damaging leak/surprise or sudden poll movement driven by Piker-related attacks.

questions.question: El-Sayed comdemn or disavow Hasan Piker before midterms?
questions.resolution_criteria:
Resolution criteria

This market will resolve to YES if, at any point before the polls close in Michigan for the U.S. midterm general election (8:00 PM EST on November 3, 2026), Dr. Abdul El-Sayed or his official campaign issues an explicit public statement that condemns, disavows, or formally distances his campaign from Twitch streamer Hasan Piker.

For a YES resolution, the statement must meet the following criteria:

Must be before the polls close in Michigan for the U.S. midterm general election (8:00 PM EST on November 3, 2026)

Must be published by a credible news organization, via an official campaign press release, or through El-Sayed’s official verified social media channels.

Must feature El-Sayed (or his campaign) explicitly condemning, or disavowing Piker, or explicitly stating regret or an apology for holding joint campaign events with him.

Bloomberg reported a private investor meeting on Oct 14 and formal marketing starting the week of Nov 9 with trading before Thanksgiving; the SEC's 15-day rule would then require a public S-1 by about Oct 23-25. The schedule has already slipped once (from mid-October), and SEC review or market conditions could push it into November, so this is close to a coin flip.

Base rate: most companies that confidentially file a draft S-1 go public within 4-6 months; Anthropic's confidential filing was 132 days ago. The Bloomberg report of a private investor meeting on Oct 14 and possible formal marketing the week of Nov 9 implies a public S-1 around Oct 23-25 under the SEC's 15-day rule, which would meet the Oct 31 deadline. However, the timeline has already slipped from mid-October marketing to November, and Anthropic has not confirmed dates, so further delays are plausible.

The base rate for companies that file a confidential S-1 is high—about 70‑80% go public within four months, implying a strong chance of a public filing by Oct 31. However, as of Oct 11 no S-1 had appeared on EDGAR, which updates the probability downward given the elapsed time. Bloomberg’s report of a private investor meeting on Oct 14 and possible marketing the week of Nov 9 suggests a roadshow that would require a public filing around Oct 23‑25 under the SEC’s 15‑day rule, which would meet the deadline, lifting the estimate somewhat. Balancing these factors yields a roughly one‑in‑four chance that Anthropic’s S-1 will be public by 31 Oct 2026.

Companies often publicly file within a few months of a confidential draft, and Bloomberg reports a timeline requiring a public S-1 by ~Oct 25 to start marketing Nov 9, which fits within the Oct 31 deadline. However, the schedule has already slipped from earlier plans, and there is no official confirmation, so a further delay is possible. I estimate a 75% chance based on a moderate base rate adjusted for the specific reported timeline and current uncertainty.

A company with a confidential S-1 and a reported late-October/early-November roadshow has a high base chance of filing publicly before the roadshow. The Oct 14 investor meeting and possible Nov 9 marketing imply a public S-1 around Oct 23-25 under the 15-day rule, which would satisfy the Oct 31 cutoff. However, the schedule has already slipped, Anthropic has not confirmed dates, and an early-November filing could still allow trading before Thanksgiving, so there is meaningful uncertainty.

Base rate for a major tech IPO whose confidential S-1 has been on file for 132+ days to make a public filing within ~3 weeks is moderate. The Bloomberg timeline implies marketing starting the week of Nov 9, which under the SEC 15-day rule requires a public S-1 by Oct 23-25—comfortably before Oct 31. However, the schedule has already slipped from earlier mid-October expectations, and Anthropic has not confirmed dates, meaning a further slip past Nov 9 marketing would push the public S-1 past the Oct 31 deadline. A shift either way (earlier or later confirmation) could move this probability significantly.

questions.question: Will Anthropic’s IPO Form S-1 be public by 31 October 2026?
questions.resolution_criteria: Resolves YES if a Form S-1 or S-1/A for Anthropic’s proposed IPO is publicly accessible on SEC EDGAR by 23:59 ET on 31 October 2026. The market needs a new emergency that actually disrupts or asserts federal control over the midterms, and legal scholars say the executive has no authority to administer elections. With 3 weeks left and no reported move by the administration, a qualifying declaration is unlikely.

Historically, presidents have almost never used the National Emergencies Act to influence elections, giving a base rate well below 5%. Trump’s allies have publicly urged such a move and he has not ruled it out, which raises the chance, but his February statement that he was not considering it and the strong legal constraints that any election‑related emergency would likely be struck down keep the probability modest. Overall, the evidence suggests a roughly 7% likelihood of a newly declared national emergency that would disrupt the 2026 midterms before the November 3 deadline.

The base rate for a president declaring a national emergency to disrupt or control midterm elections is essentially zero historically. Trump's February denial and subsequent non-committal 'stranger things have happened' remark, combined with no concrete steps as of mid-October, suggest a low probability. Legal challenges and the strict market criteria (requiring practical disruption, not just routine sanctions) further reduce the likelihood, though Trump's unpredictability and Bannon's influence leave a small tail risk.

Base rate: Declaring a national emergency to assert federal control over elections is unprecedented and legally dubious, making the prior very low. Evidence: Trump explicitly disavowed the idea in February, and while he refused to rule it out in August under pressure from allies, no concrete action has materialized with only three weeks until the deadline. What would change it: A sudden escalation in Trump's rhetoric alleging foreign interference or voting fraud in the final weeks would substantially increase the probability.

The main upward evidence is his refusal to rule it out and pressure from Bannon and Root, but legal constraints, likely court challenges, and the absence of an imminent draft order keep the probability modest. A sudden announcement, leaked order, or explicit threat would materially raise the estimate.

Base rate for Trump declaring a new national emergency is moderate given his history of using emergency powers, but the specific requirement that it must disrupt or assert federal authority over midterms is a much higher bar. Trump publicly said in February 2026 he was not considering such a move, and while he declined to rule it out in August, legal scholars note it would face immediate court challenges and likely fail. The political cost of overtly federalizing elections before midterms is high even for Trump, and allies' rhetoric doesn't necessarily translate to action. A last-minute October surprise declaration remains possible but unlikely given the legal and political obstacles.

questions.question: Will Trump declare a national emergency before the midterms?
questions.resolution_criteria:
Shadow strategist Bannon seems to believe so. 

Resolution criteria

This market resolves to YES if Donald Trump, in his capacity as President of the United States, officially declares a new national emergency under the National Emergencies Act (50 U.S.C. 1601 et seq.) on or before November 3, 2026 (11:59 PM EST).

Source of Truth: The declaration must be officially published as a Presidential Proclamation or Executive Order on the Federal Register (federalregister.gov) or the official White House website (whitehouse.gov).

Exclusions: This market requires a newly declared national emergency. The continuation, extension, or modification of existing national emergencies (such as the January 2025 emergency regarding energy and critical minerals) will not qualify.

If no qualifying new national emergency is officially declared by the deadline, the market resolves to NO.

Background

In July and August 2026, key allies of Donald Trump—including former White House strategist Steve Bannon and media host Wayne Allyn Root—publicly urged the President to declare a national security emergency to assert federal control over the upcoming 2026 midterm elections. Proponents of this move suggest it could be used to implement voting restrictions, such as strict photo ID and citizenship requirements, or station ICE agents at polling places.

Legal scholars and critics have heavily disputed the legality of such an action, noting that the U.S. Constitution explicitly grants individual states and Congress—not the executive branch—the authority to administer federal elections. Trump himself has publicly declined to rule out the idea, stating in an August 2026 interview that "stranger things have happened" when asked about declaring an election-related emergency.

Update 2026-08-22 (PST) (AI summary of creator comment): To resolve to YES, any newly declared national emergency must have the effect of disrupting the midterms.

Routine declarations (such as foreign sanctions) will not qualify unless they disrupt the midterms.

The mechanism of disruption matters less than the declaration itself.

Update 2026-08-23 (PST) (AI summary of creator comment): * The market's subtext (disrupting or asserting control over the midterms) governs the resolution criteria.

Routine trade or foreign sanctions (such as Cuba- or Venezuela-style sanctions) will not qualify for a YES resolution.

Update 2026-08-24 (PST) (AI summary of creator comment): - A qualifying declaration must have the practical effect of disrupting or asserting federal authority over the midterms, regardless of its stated basis (such as using foreign interference as a pretext).

Routine foreign sanctions or trade declarations do not qualify.

Final resolution is subject to creator judgment.
